title: Proper marked curve contractions and exceptional trees
statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure] and $(C',D')$, $(C,D)$ proper multipointed $k$-curves [def-trf-multipointed-curve, def-weil-proper-morphism] with reduced underlying curves [def-pc-reduced-scheme]. Let $f:C'\to C$ be a proper surjective $k$-morphism and $f_D:D'\to D$ a compatible morphism of markings. The marking schemes are finite over $k$ [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism]. Assume equal arithmetic genera
$$p_a(C')=p_a(C),\qquad p_a(X)=1-\chi(X,\mathcal O_X)$$
with Euler characteristic [def-pc-euler-characteristic]. Let $x\in C(k)$, let $Z=C'\times_C\operatorname{Spec}k$ be the scheme-theoretic fibre [def-pc-scheme-fibre], and assume $Z$ is a nonempty connected curve of pure dimension one [def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-pure-dimension]. Suppose $f:C'\setminus Z\to C\setminus\{x\}$ is an isomorphism and $(C',D')$ is semistable at every point of $Z$ [def-trf-semistable-multipointed-pair]. For the local marking length, let $A_x=\mathcal O_{D,x}$ be the local Artinian factor of the finite marking algebra at $x$ when $x\in D$, and $A_x=0$ when $x\notin D$. Assume its conservation:
$$\dim_k A_x=|D'\cap Z|.$$
(The empty marking contributes zero; intersections and counts use distinct $k$-points.) Define $\partial(Z)=|Z|\cap\overline{|C'|\setminus|Z|}$ in $C'$. Then $(C,D)$ is semistable at $x$ if and only if $Z$ is an exceptional projective-line tree: $Z$ is reduced and nodal, each of its reduced irreducible components [def-weil-irreducible-components] is isomorphic over $k$ to $\mathbf P^1_k$ [def-nagata-projective-space-base-change], its finite incidence multigraph (one vertex per component, one edge per node, including loops at self-nodes) is a tree, and
$$|\partial(Z)|+|D'\cap Z|\le2.$$
Nodal means that every nonsmooth closed point [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] has completed local $k$-algebra $k[[u,v]]/(uv)$ [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion, def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. A tree is a connected finite graph without cycles, with loops and parallel edges counted as cycles. The scheme-theoretic fibre is retained in the conclusion; it is not silently replaced by its reduction.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.2 after the local-to-projective reduction, printed pp. 30--31, using Appendix B Corollary B.2 and the definition of boundary on printed pp. 56--57.

proof.text: Put $B=Z_{\mathrm{red}}$. Its support equals that of $Z$, so it is nonempty, connected, pure of dimension one and has the same boundary and marking counts. The reduced-subscheme node supplies this structure. By the nodal-subcurve-boundary lemma, applied to $B\subset C'$ and the semistable neighbourhood supplied by the hypothesis, $B$ is nodal; its boundary is a finite reduced set, smooth on $B$, with one ambient node per boundary point. Write $v$ for its number of components, $e$ for its internal nodes, and $n$ for its boundary points. Let $g_i$ be the genus of the normalization of its $i$-th reduced component; the normalization-genus lemma supplies smooth proper connected normalizations and finiteness.

source.place: Appendix B, definitions following Lemma B.1 and setup of Corollary B.2, p. 57; reduction introduced only for the intermediate calculation.

proof.text: Apply the normalization-branches lemma to $f$, $x$ and $B$. All its hypotheses are the properness, reducedness, pure dimensions, connected positive-dimensional fibre, isomorphism off that fibre, and nodal neighbourhood stipulated here. It identifies the normalizations of all noncontracted components with those of $C$. It identifies the normalization points of $C$ above $x$ bijectively with $\partial(B)$, so the branch number at $x$ is $n$ and $n\ge1$.

source.place: Corollary B.2 proof, last paragraph, p. 58.

proof.text:
Subtract the normalization-genus formulas for $C'$ and $C$. The noncontracted normalized component genera cancel by the preceding identification; the number of components of $C'$ exceeds that of $C$ by $v$. The local delta terms off $B$ cancel because $f$ is an isomorphism there. At points of $B$, the only nonsmooth ambient points are its $e$ internal nodes and its $n$ boundary nodes. The ordinary-point-delta lemma gives delta $1$ at each node and $0$ at each smooth point. Consequently
$$p_a(C')-p_a(C)=-v+\sum_i g_i+e+n-\delta_C(x).$$
The assumed equal genera therefore give $\delta_C(x)=n-1+(e-v+1)+\sum_i g_i$.

source.place: Corollary B.2 proof, genus-formula subtraction, p. 58.

proof.text: The incidence multigraph of $B$ is connected: a partition of its vertices with no crossing node would partition $B$ into two disjoint unions of its finitely many closed components, each also open, contrary to connectedness. For any finite connected multigraph on $v$ vertices, successively adding an edge to a new vertex from the vertices already reached produces a spanning tree with $v-1$ edges. Thus $e-v+1\ge0$, with equality exactly when there are no additional edges, that is, when the graph itself is a tree. Each $g_i$ is a vector-space dimension, hence nonnegative. It follows from the preceding equality that $\delta_C(x)=n-1$ exactly when the graph is a tree and every $g_i=0$.

source.place: Appendix B, Corollary B.2 proof, graph count, p. 58; explicit finite spanning-tree argument.

proof.text: If the graph is a tree, there are no self-nodes, so every component of $B$ is smooth: at a node incident with another component its reduced single-branch local ring is smooth, while all other points were already smooth on $B$. This single-branch assertion is also the smooth-boundary clause of the nodal-subcurve lemma applied to that component. By the smooth-normal lemma, these smooth components are normal, so their normalizations are themselves (their local rings already equal their integral closures). The genus-zero-smooth-proper-line lemma then identifies each component with $\mathbf P^1_k$ when $g_i=0$. Conversely, components isomorphic to $\mathbf P^1_k$ have genus zero by the projective-line-genus-zero lemma. Hence the condition in Step 4 is exactly the projective-line-tree condition for $B$.

source.place: Appendix B, definition of projective-line tree after Lemma B.1, p. 57; Stacks 0C6U genus-zero characterization.

proof.text: The ordinary-point-delta lemma applied at $x$, using its branch number $n$ from Step 2, now says that $x$ is an ordinary $n$-fold point exactly when $B$ is a projective-line tree. In either of these equivalent cases the reduced-fibre clause of the normalization-branches lemma gives $Z=B$. Therefore the same equivalence holds with the actual scheme-theoretic fibre $Z$, including its reducedness. In particular a semistable curve point gives $n=1$ (smooth) or $n=2$ (node), and conversely an ordinary point with $n\le2$ is a semistable curve point.

source.place: Appendix B, Corollary B.2 and ordinary-point characterization, pp. 56--58; reduced-fibre comparison made explicit.

proof.text: Put $m=|D'\cap Z|$. The local marking-length hypothesis gives $\dim_k A_x=m$. At the fixed $k$-point $x$, the local marking factor is either empty or a local finite $k$-scheme supported at that one point, since $D\hookrightarrow C$ is a closed immersion. It is empty when $m=0$, since a nonzero local Artinian $k$-algebra has positive dimension. For $m=1$ its unital $k$-algebra is one-dimensional, hence the scalar map $k\to A_x$ is an isomorphism. Conversely, the etale-algebra-over-field-product lemma expresses an etale local marking algebra as a product of finite separable field extensions of $k$. Locality selects one factor, and algebraic closure identifies it with $k$, so its length is one. Thus at a smooth $x$ the marking is allowed exactly for $m=0$ or $1$; at a node semistability requires the marking to be absent, hence $m=0$. These are precisely the marking and smooth-locus requirements in the semistable-pair definition. Here $A_x$ is the local Artinian factor of the finite scheme $D$ at $x$, rather than the fibre of the closed immersion $D\hookrightarrow C$: localization of a finite-dimensional algebra at a maximal ideal selects that factor.

source.place: Temkin §1.2 semistable markings, p. 2, and Appendix B exceptional marking count, p. 58; elementary local marking-algebra argument.

proof.text: Since $n\ge1$, the inequality $n+m\le2$ has exactly the possibilities $(n,m)=(1,0),(1,1),(2,0)$. Steps 6 and 7 say that these are exactly the semistable marked target cases, together with the projective-line-tree condition for the scheme-theoretic fibre. Boundary and marking counts for $B$ and $Z$ agree by Step 1. This proves both directions of the stated equivalence.

source.place: Appendix B marked exceptional-tree condition, p. 58; final numerical assembly.

proof_origin.place: Primary PDF read online, Appendix B pp. 56--58; local archival copy absent. Expansion of the genus calculation, marking-length condition and scheme-fibre comparison.

lean.statement: theorem curve_p1_tree_local_criterion {k : Type u} [Field k] [IsAlgClosed k] (P' P : MultipointedCurve (Spec (.of k))) [IsProper P'.x] [IsProper P.x] [IsReduced P'.X] [IsReduced P.X] [IsFinite P'.d] [IsFinite P.d] (f : P'.X ⟶ P.X) (fD : P'.D ⟶ P.D) (hf : f ≫ P.x = P'.x) (hfD : fD ≫ P.d = P'.d) (hmark : fD ≫ P.i = P'.i ≫ f) [IsProper f] [Surjective f] (hgenus : 1 - @Scheme.Modules.eulerChar k _ P'.X ⟨P'.x⟩ (SheafOfModules.unit P'.X.ringCatSheaf) = 1 - @Scheme.Modules.eulerChar k _ P.X ⟨P.x⟩ (SheafOfModules.unit P.X.ringCatSheaf)) (x : P.X) (hx : IsClosed ({x} : Set P.X)) [ConnectedSpace (f.fiber x)] (hpure : (f.fiber x).IsPureDimension 1) (hoff : IsIso (pullback.snd f (Scheme.Opens.ι (X := P.X) ⟨{x}ᶜ, hx.isOpen_compl⟩))) (hsemi : ∀ z : f.fiber x, (MultipointedPair.ofCurve P').IsSemistableAt (f.fiberι x z)) (hlength : (P.localMarkingLength x : ℕ∞) = (Set.range P'.i ∩ Set.range (f.fiberι x)).encard) : (MultipointedPair.ofCurve P).IsSemistableAt x ↔ IsProjectiveLineTree (f.fiberι x ≫ P'.x) ∧ (Set.range (f.fiberι x) ∩ closure (Set.range (f.fiberι x))ᶜ).encard + (Set.range P'.i ∩ Set.range (f.fiberι x)).encard ≤ 2
lean.note: Closed points encode k-points via Mathlib pointEquivClosedPoint. The residue-field fibre retains its scheme structure and its k-map f.fiberι x ≫ P′.x. The finite connected incidence multigraph is a tree exactly when its actual node count plus one equals its component count; no simple-graph quotient is used.
